reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The 44 projected home runs and 39 steals in the same season is the headline, but the Statcast profile is what makes it credible. His xSLG sits at .502 with a 13.2% barrel rate and 49.0% hard-hit rate, both in the top tenth of the league, while an 11.6% walk rate keeps the .372 OBP honest even with a 26.1% strikeout rate that is well above average. The chase rate at 33.9% is the one thing that could unravel the whole profile — if pitchers find a consistent way to expand him and that K% climbs further, the contact floor gets uncomfortable fast. But if the current discipline-and-damage balance holds, this is a true five-category force with ceiling to spare.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The .489 xSLG is the real engine here, sitting comfortably above most of the league, and it comes attached to a 91.3 mph average exit velocity and 12.6% barrel rate that explain why the raw pop keeps showing up. Merrill's a legitimate power-speed threat, with the projection seeing 27 home runs and 28 stolen bags across 668 PA, and his 29.0 ft/s sprint speed backs both numbers. The tension in the profile is the approach: a 36.9% chase rate and 6.3% walk rate mean he's getting himself out more than he needs to, which is why that .266 xBA doesn't fully cash the xSLG's promise and the OBP projection sits at .300. If the contact and discipline tighten even modestly, you're looking at a legitimate middle-of-the-order piece; if the chase rate stays where it is, he's a productive, slightly frustrating everyday player who carries fantasy value on counting stats and limits his own ceiling.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .480 and the barrel rate at 12.9%, and those two numbers together explain almost everything about this profile. The exit velocity is ordinary at 90.2 mph, so the pop is coming from contact quality and barrel location, not raw brute force, which is a finer skill than it looks and one that tends to carry. The projection puts him at 34 home runs and a .814 OPS in a full 702 PA season, and the Statcast contact metrics, with xwOBA at .350 and xSLG clearing his projected SLG, say that's not a ceiling but a floor if the barrel rate holds. At 22, the whole read hinges on whether he keeps finding barrels as the league adjusts, because the speed (26.6 ft/s) and defense (27th-percentile OAA) leave no margin elsewhere.

reports.name: Jackson Chourio
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the chase rate tell two completely different stories. Chourio's exit velocity sits at 91.7 mph and his barrel rate is 12.4%, both in the upper tier of the league, but he's chasing at 34.2%, a rate that puts him near the bottom quarter of qualified hitters. His xSLG of .477 says the power is translating when he makes contact; the question is how many at-bats he gives away before he does. The ValuCast projection (.292/.347/.495, 26 HR) assumes enough contact quality to carry the discipline problem, and at 22 that's a reasonable bet, but if the chase rate doesn't come down as pitchers map his tendencies, the .292 fades and you're left with a .260 hitter who still hits the ball hard when he connects.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 38.3% strikeout rate at the MLB level is the kind of number that ends arguments. Misiorowski's xERA sits at 2.10, his whiff rate at 37.4%, and the 100.6 mph fastball with 2633 rpm spin explains both: hitters aren't just missing, they're missing badly, and when they do make contact the barrel rate is 3.9%. If the 6.7% walk rate holds anywhere near that mark across a full 178.2 projected innings, you're looking at a genuine ace. The dependency is command: if BB% climbs and he loses the ability to expand the zone after getting ahead, the strikeout-to-walk shape softens and what's left is considerably more ordinary.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact metrics against him as a pitcher tell the story cleanly: a 2.73 xERA, 3.8% barrel rate allowed, and 87.4 mph average exit velocity surrendered, all sitting in the top quarter of the league or better. As a hitter, the .399 xwOBA and 15.8% barrel rate are what you'd expect from a man whose 51.5% hard-hit rate is genuinely elite, and a 13.4% walk rate keeps the on-base floor high even when his 31.5% whiff rate bleeds into the strikeout column. The projection puts him at .277/.380/.524 with 32 home runs across 627 PA, which probably undersells the ceiling if he logs a full two-way workload, and the floor here is not a talent question but a health and usage one: how many innings does Dodger management actually hand him. There is no version of this Statcast profile that reads as ordinary.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP at 18 years old, across three levels including Double-A, is the whole argument. Willits has walked 95 times against 112 strikeouts in 532 plate appearances across AA & A+ & A, a discipline profile that translates to a 12.8% walk rate in MLB context, well above the league mean. The power is the open question: his .191 ISO across AA & A+ & A softens to a .130 MLB equivalent, below average, which means the everyday-regular ceiling runs through the on-base skill holding and the bat speed developing rather than through present thump. Sixty stolen bases sweeten the floor, but if the power doesn't grow, what's left is a high-OBP, plus-speed table-setter who lands closer to a bench or depth outcome than the top of the lineup.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

The 31.4% strikeout rate sits at the 96th percentile, the 98.0 mph fastball with 2533 rpm of spin explains how he generates it, and a 6.0% walk rate keeps the profile clean enough that hitters rarely get to work around the swing-and-miss. The one genuine wrinkle is contact quality: his 39.7% hard-hit rate and barrel rate at the 42nd percentile suggest the stuff that misses bats doesn't necessarily play weak when it gets hit, so if the chase rate (34.3%) dips or hitters make better decisions, the ERA closes toward the xERA of 2.91 rather than the headline number. Even at the xERA, that's a front-of-the-rotation arm.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely elite, and yet the power has gone somewhere. A 93rd-percentile xBA against a 6.7% barrel rate tells the whole tension: Guerrero Jr. is making excellent contact, he's just stopped hitting the ball with authority when it matters most, with xSLG sitting exactly at the median. The projection's .364 SLG over 625 PA would be a quiet, almost invisible number for someone with his pedigree, and it holds up if the current shape of his swing holds, which is the one thing this read hinges on. If the barrel rate climbs back toward what he showed in his peak years, the .284 xBA becomes a monster foundation; if it doesn't, what's left is a well-disciplined, slow-footed first baseman with a 13.0% strikeout rate and not nearly enough thump to carry the position.

reports.name: Termarr Johnson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and also the most complicated. At AAA in 2026, Termarr Johnson has drawn 68 walks against 101 strikeouts across 406 plate appearances, and that 17% walk rate translates to 13.1% at the MLB level, where most hitters sit around 8.5%. The power, though, is a different story: his .120 ISO at AAA translates to .114 in the majors, well short of the .150 MLB average, and a .199 average sitting on a .259 BABIP suggests the contact isn't beating defenders when it lands. The 24 stolen bases at AAA matter here, because if the legs can manufacture value that the bat isn't yet providing, the floor stays livable, but everything hinges on whether the contact quality catches up enough to make opposing pitchers respect the plate discipline instead of just pitching around it. Right now the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is the same.

reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
reports.published_report:
The xwOBA is 89th percentile. The xSLG is 86th percentile. The projection says .787 OPS across 483 plate appearances, and that gap between what the contact quality promises and what the actual output delivers is the whole Acuña story right now.

The whiff rate is sitting at the 21st percentile, which is the drag on everything: the barrel rate and hard-hit numbers say the bat-to-ball contact is still quality when it happens, but a 29.7% whiff rate bleeds enough plate appearances to keep the counting stats modest, with 19 home runs and 23 steals projecting as the floor of a guy who once looked like a perennial MVP conversation piece.

The sprint speed at 27.2 ft/s, 44th percentile, is the other thing to watch; if the legs aren't what they were pre-injury, the stolen base projection leans on opportunity and instincts more than pure burst. What remains is a legitimate middle-of-the-order quality hitter whose 11.5% walk rate keeps the OBP functional even when the whiff rate spikes, and whose ceiling depends almost entirely on whether the contact consistency returns.

reports.name: Didier Fuentes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.97 and the strikeout rate is 31.5%, both of which describe a reliever who already belongs in high-leverage conversations. Fuentes gets there by missing bats at a 30.2% whiff rate while throwing 97.2 mph, and the xwOBA of .268 says the contact he does allow is getting suppressed for real reasons. The vulnerability is the fastball spin sitting at 2101 rpm, well below league average, which means the heater's effectiveness depends on something other than ride, and if hitters adjust to that shape the strikeout rate is the first thing that softens. At 21 years old in Atlanta's pen, he's projecting for 73.3 innings and a 2.37 ERA, and if the stuff translates cleanly he's a genuine high-leverage piece; if the low-spin fastball gets decoded, what's left is a functional middle reliever.

reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: The fastball grades out beautifully, 96.9 mph with 2334 rpm spin, and then the hard-hit numbers arrive to complicate everything. A 44.4% hard-hit rate that low in the percentile distribution tells you hitters are squaring him up when they do make contact, and the 23.0% whiff rate isn't doing enough to hide it. The Statcast profile lands at a 4.24 xERA, which is about where the projection settles him too, around 4.47 over 152.9 innings. He's a starter with a genuine fastball who doesn't miss enough bats to neutralize the contact quality, and whether that changes depends entirely on whether he finds a way to generate more weak contact, because if he doesn't, the stuff-to-results gap stays flat and he's a back-end innings-eater on the Milwaukee staff.

reports.name: Casey Mize
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.47 with a walk rate of 6.0%, and that pairing is the whole argument for Mize: he doesn't beat hitters, he just refuses to beat himself. The chase rate is 29.3% and the whiff rate is 24.3%, neither one doing much to scare a lineup, which means the contact management has to hold, and it's been holding, with barrel rate and hard-hit rate both running below the levels you'd expect from a guy giving up this much contact. If those contact numbers regress toward his pedestrian exit-velocity profile, the 3.47 xERA becomes a fiction and you're left with a 135-inning arm who can't finish counts. At his best he's a solid mid-rotation piece who earns his projected 3.77 ERA through cleanliness; at his worst he's an innings-eater with a thin margin for error.

Harper gets there the old-fashioned way: a 16.2% walk rate that matches xwOBA at the 98th percentile, paired with a 30.5% whiff rate that looks ugly in isolation but hasn't stopped him from making enough hard contact to post a .492 xSLG. The raw exit velocity at 90.5 mph is solid rather than elite, which means the projection of 30 home runs leans on his ability to find the barrel consistently rather than brute force. At 33, he's a walk-dependent, on-base machine with plus power, not a peak-tool athlete, and the profile holds as long as the plate discipline does.

reports.name: Braylon Doughty
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. Across AA & A+, Doughty has issued just 25 walks in 104.4 innings, a 2.2 BB/9 that translates to 2.7 in MLB terms, comfortably under the MLB average of 3.2. That kind of command at 20 is the thing you can't teach, and the 1.3 WHIP says it's showing up in results. The strikeout side is more modest, 114 punchouts across AA & A+ translating to a 7.9 K/9 where the average MLB starter sits at 8.6, so this isn't a swing-and-miss profile riding a hot stretch, which is exactly why the ceiling lands at multi-inning reliever or setup role rather than something grander. If the command holds as he climbs, he's a useful late-inning weapon; if the stuff doesn't gain enough to bump that K rate, the floor is a depth arm who misses bats just often enough to stay on a roster.

reports.name: Connor Prielipp

Hitters are getting to his stuff when they make contact, and a 4.12 xERA suggests the peripherals aren't far off from true average, even if the projected 5.08 ERA looks punitive. The profile hinges almost entirely on whether the hard contact suppression improves, because without it, 130 projected strikeouts across 121.5 innings buys you a back-end starter who stays in rotation by the skin of his wins total. Right now he's a fifth starter who needs something to give.

reports.name: Edward Florentino
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in this profile. The walk rate tells a complementary story: 76 walks, a 16% clip that would translate to 11.7% in the majors, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average. What you're betting on is whether the contact rate gets there, because a 26% strikeout rate here translates to 29.2% up the ladder, and a .235 average with a .264 BABIP doesn't leave much cushion if the swing-and-miss doesn't come down. If the power holds and the contact improves even modestly, there's a regular here; if it doesn't, the walks and speed keep him relevant as a bench piece, but the ceiling narrows fast.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The gap between his contact quality and his actual contact is the whole tension in this profile. Hernández barrels up 13.9% of batted balls with a 91.5 mph average exit velocity, numbers that put him in elite company for raw damage, yet his 33.2% whiff rate drags the xBA all the way down to .247 while the xSLG sits at .490 — two numbers that don't usually coexist. The .226 projection average is honest about that: he makes hard contact when he connects, but a 27.0% strikeout rate at the projected 492 PA means there's real leakage between the power and the batting line. If he trims the whiff rate, that .490 xSLG has a path to actual production; if he doesn't, you're looking at a .763 OPS corner outfielder who earns his lineup spot on power and little else.

reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile here is deliberately, almost stubbornly modest — 88.2 mph average exit velocity, a 5.8% barrel rate, an xSLG of .380, and yet the projection lands at 27 home runs across 722 plate appearances. That's not a contradiction so much as a thesis: Bregman is a volume, discipline, and pitch-selection machine, not a masher. A 23.5% chase rate and 15.8% whiff rate are both legitimately elite, and a 15.0% strikeout rate means he keeps the at-bat alive long enough to make the walk, 10.7%, do real work. The profile holds together as long as he stays healthy enough to eat those 722 plate appearances, because the power isn't coming from a thunderous swing; it's coming from a refusal to give anything away.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.95 and the xwOBA at .267, both in the 90th percentile, built almost entirely on contact suppression rather than swing-and-miss. Miles gets barrels at a 3.6% rate, 96th percentile, and holds average exit velocity to 86.8 mph, which explains why the underlying numbers look this clean despite a Whiff% of 18.5% that sits near the bottom of the league. reports.name: Jacob Latz

His 30.4% whiff rate and 35.1% chase rate explain how he gets there: hitters are swinging at his stuff out of the zone and missing it in it, which keeps hard contact from ever becoming the issue. The walk rate at 8.5% is the thing to watch — it's roughly league average, and if it drifts north, the margin for error in a closer's role gets thin fast. At a projected 31 saves and 0.82 WHIP, he profiles as a genuine late-inning anchor for Texas rather than a saves-opportunity dependent mirage.

reports.name: Cal Raleigh

The 13.4% walk rate keeps him from being purely a hack-and-hope profile, but a 31.0% strikeout rate and a 35.7% chase rate mean pitchers have a clear and repeatable plan against him. reports.name: Sterlin Thompson
reports.published_report: The .473 OBP at AAA is the headline, but the translation is where it gets complicated. Across 370 plate appearances at AAA in 2026, Thompson has drawn 70 walks against just 58 strikeouts, and the MLB-equivalent read puts his walk rate at 14.3%, nearly double what a typical major leaguer posts, while his translated ISO lands right at the league-average neighborhood of .152. That's the tension: elite strike-zone judgment, fringy power, and a .374 BABIP propping up the .325 batting average. If the contact quality doesn't translate and that BABIP regresses hard, what's left is a patient left-handed bat with average pop, which is a bench piece, not a regular.

Across 107 innings at AAA, Tong has posted a 5.0 BB/9 that softens to a 4.6 BB/9 MLB equivalent — meaningful, because MLB pitchers average 3.2, and his translated K-BB% of 12.1% lands just under the 13.5% MLB average despite strikeout stuff that plays close to serviceable. The 126 strikeouts in 107 AAA innings give the swing-and-miss some real shape, but if the command doesn't tighten at the next level he's a depth arm with a good day job. Ceiling and floor are basically the same thing here: a depth option who gets called when someone gets hurt, and goes back when they don't.

reports.name: Ryan Cesarini

Cesarini is slugging .560 across AA & A+ with a .27 ISO, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his isolated power at .179, a figure that would give most major-league outfields something to think about. reports.name: Tommy Troy
reports.published_report: The .413 BABIP is doing a lot of work here, and that's the whole conversation. Troy is hitting .313/.411/.468 across 237 AAA plate appearances in 2026, with 32 walks and 55 strikeouts, and the contact profile ranks 97th percentile among the hitter pool — but translated to MLB level, the ISO shrinks to .136 while the MLB average sits at .150, which means if that BABIP regresses toward earth, there isn't enough pop to hold the line. The walk rate translates to 10.6% at the big-league level, a meaningful step past the MLB average of 8.5%, so the plate discipline is genuine currency, but this profile hinges entirely on whether the hit tool is real enough to sustain a BABIP that currently looks like a hot stretch more than a skill. On a rehab assignment at Reno, he's organizational depth unless the contact proves it can travel.

reports.name: Eric Bitonti
reports.published_report: The power and the plate discipline are both loud, and the strikeout rate is the whole argument. Across AA & A+, Bitonti has 25 home runs, 82 walks, and a .248 ISO against 169 strikeouts in 507 plate appearances — the kind of profile where the tools are obviously there and the contact rate is obviously a problem. Translated to MLB, that 33% minor-league strikeout rate becomes something closer to 36%, and that's a number a first baseman with no defensive home has to somehow survive. If he tightens the zone enough to keep the walks and power without the strikeout rate eating him alive, there's a second-division regular here; if the contact doesn't come, the walk rate and raw power leave a bench bat who plays once a week against righties.

reports.name: Ian Seymour
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the spine of this profile: 35.1% puts him in the 90th percentile, and he converts that into strikeouts at 28.8%, which is legitimately elite company. When hitters are chasing at that clip and whiffing on 29.2% of swings, the .295 xwOBA and 3.63 xERA start to make sense, even against a fastball sitting 91.4 mph that rates near the bottom of the league. That velocity floor is the thing — if hitters learn to lay off or simply punish a below-average heater without the element of surprise, the deception-dependent strikeout rate compresses and that 10.0% barrel rate becomes the number running the show instead of the chase rate. If the arsenal holds, he's a back-end starter who outperforms his stuff; if it doesn't, the 4.31 ERA projection looks closer to floor than ceiling.

reports.name: Ethan Salas
reports.published_report: The contact is the lead. The power hasn't followed: a .152 ISO across those same levels translates to .129 at the MLB equivalent, and if it stays there, the profile leans entirely on whether elite contact alone can carry a catcher's offensive load. reports.name: Will Warren
reports.published_report: The fastball spin, 2539 rpm at the 91st percentile, is the loudest thing in this profile and it's surrounded almost entirely by bad news. Hitters are barreling him up at a 44.2% hard-hit rate, average exit velocity sits at 90.8 mph, and the xERA of 4.48 says the current ERA projection of 4.05 is doing him a favor. The strikeout and walk rates are league-average territory, the whiff and chase numbers are below it, and there's no secondary skill in this Statcast card that explains how the spin translates into outs, which means the whole profile hinges on whether he can find a way to weaponize that spin rather than just generate hard contact with a decent-looking fastball. If that connection gets made, you have a back-end starter who eats 159.5 innings; if it doesn't, 9 quality starts is the ceiling, not a baseline.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost uniformly bad, and that's the whole tension here. A 5.36 xERA, a 16.7% strikeout rate, a 19.8% whiff rate — this is a pitcher who doesn't miss bats and gives up hard contact at a 41.8% clip, with a 91.8 mph fastball that hitters pick up early. The one genuine asset is a 6.6% walk rate, outstanding control that buys margin, but control without swing-and-miss is a narrower margin for error than the 3.94 projected ERA implies. If he maintains the strike-throwing and adds nothing else, he's a back-end innings-eater who lives in danger every fifth day, the floor looks like a reliever who gets stretched, and the ceiling is a fringe rotation piece who navigates by location alone.

reports.name: Tristan Peters
reports.published_report: The Statcast card tells you exactly who he is: a plus runner with elite defense who does not hit the ball hard. Sprint speed at 28.6 ft/s and a 96th-percentile OAA grade give him a genuine everyday argument on the non-bat side, but 87.5 mph average exit velocity and a 33.8% hard-hit rate both sit in the bottom quarter of the league, and his 32.4% chase rate means he's giving pitchers a short count to exploit the soft contact. The .317 xwOBA at the 43rd percentile is where the bat actually lives, not the .276/.342/.457 projection line, which leans on his speed and contact volume to get there. If the glove plays every day on a team that values it, he profiles as a reasonable regular; if the exit-velocity floor catches up to him at the plate, the defensive value alone supports a strong bench piece rather than someone who needs 492 PA to justify a roster spot.

At AAA in 2026, Cross is striking out at a 31% clip across 448 plate appearances, and that translates to a 29.8% mark against MLB pitching, well above the league rate of 22.0%. The power reads fine at .193 ISO, but the MLB-equivalent lands right at the league-average ISO line, which means the bat has to carry itself almost entirely on raw thump with almost no margin for the contact issues to improve. His 7.0% MLB-equivalent walk rate trails the 8.5% league figure, so there's no patience profile cushioning the strikeouts. If the swing decisions tighten, he's a bench outfielder with usable pop; if they don't, the floor is organizational depth.

reports.name: Braxton Bragg
reports.published_report: The ratios are loud. A 27% K-BB% at AA with a 2.5 BB/9 is an unusually clean control profile for a level where most arms are still negotiating the strike zone. Across AA & A+, the MLB translation puts his K-BB% at 15.8% against a 13.5% MLB baseline, and his walk rate lands just below 3.2. The catch is 42.7 innings, a prior-season sample, and a ceiling that doesn't stretch past depth arm — if the control holds in a larger upper-level stint, he's a functional big-league reliever; if it doesn't, the ERA and WHIP figures here become a small-sample number and the profile shrinks to organizational depth.

reports.name: Jared Dickey
reports.published_report: The discipline is loud and the bat is quiet. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Dickey has drawn 61 walks against 77 strikeouts in 466 plate appearances, and those translate to an 11.0% walk rate and a 19.2% strikeout rate at the MLB level — both better than league average, which is the whole profile. The power isn't there: a .125 ISO at his level translates to .113 MLB-equivalent, well short of what a corner outfielder needs to hold a lineup spot. If the contact develops into something beyond a .250 average against soft competition, the plate discipline gives him a bench floor; if it doesn't, he's a patient out with organizational depth written on the ceiling.

reports.name: Conor Essenburg
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that keeps the ceiling conversation short. Across A+ & A in 415 plate appearances, Essenburg has drawn 83 walks against 120 strikeouts, a 20% walk rate that translates to roughly 13.5% at the MLB level, while the power (17 home runs, .239 ISO) melts to a .148 MLB-equivalent, indistinguishable from a typical big leaguer. The discipline is genuine and rare for a 19-year-old; the problem is that a 32.9% translated strikeout rate attached to average-equivalent power is a profile built for depth rather than impact, and if the contact doesn't develop as he climbs, the walks become the whole argument for a roster spot. Either a patient bench bat who earns playing time with his on-base ability, or a fringe name if the strikeouts harden against better stuff.

reports.name: Matthew Lugo
reports.published_report: The power translates, but just barely. Across AAA & AA this season, Lugo is sitting at .265/.350/.473 with 14 home runs in 406 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent ISO lands at .158, right at league average, after the level discount eats into the .208 he's posting in the minors. That's the whole tension: the raw production looks like a fringy regular, but the translated profile is a guy who hits about as hard as a replacement-level big leaguer and strikes out at 25.9% against a league rate closer to 22. The walk rate survives translation almost intact, 8.7% versus the 8.5% average, which keeps him from being a total free swinger, but there's not enough on-base upside to carry a strikeout problem that big. Either he's a bench bat with pop who earns at-bats against lefties, or he's organizational depth at 25 with a ceiling that's already visible.
